rv.q: It ain’t Chicago but it’s delicately balances these darker hard not to smile.
Director Maria Friedman orchestrates this sometimes episodic play with feeling and craft.
This show may all move a little slowly but it is free of pretension, has several wry moments and I enjoyed it.
There are matchingly accomplished turns wherever you look, which, given the sitcom sketchiness of the writing, is no mean feat.
But sequins or no sequins, if it were any more middle-of-the-road you could tarmac it in place and use it as a traffic island.
There's very little substance either in characterisations or the episodic plot, and it's all far creakier than my knees.

It’s always heartening to see women taking over the West End. Stepping Out isn’t a great play but it is entertaining.
It's a small play with a big heart.
It’s just a pity that these women don’t feel more than suggestions of real people: clichés cloud the roles.

The exposition is at times clunky – you always know when somebody is Saying Something Important – and having 10 main characters means there's little time to expand the dancers' stories, which are left without resolution.
Maria Friedman's glorious production will undoubtedly help it on its way.

cn.t: This warm-hearted '80s comedy about a tap-dancing class charms with its period detail and ensemble cast, but critics find the material thin and dated, offering genial entertainment without much substance.
